The professional sand sculptor
Matt Long
spends most of the summer carving castles along the Jersey Shore and Coney Island, but he saves spaghetti omelets, guitar playing and gardening for Sunday. The 59-year-old has been featured on the Travel Channel’s “
Sand Masters
,” is the founder of the online shop
Can You Dig It Sand Tools
, competes in international sand sculpturing events, and has been hired by companies to erect elaborate designs, most recently a plane in Wildwood Crest, N.J., to promote the new Disney movie “
Planes: Fire and Rescue
.” “Unless someone requests the Taj Mahal or something, I just make sand castles up as I go,” he said. Mr. Long lives in West Brighton, Staten Island, with his wife, Nina, 59, and his daughters, Katrina, 34; Madeline, 26; and Emily, 21.
EARLY TO RISE
I get up about 5:30, 6 the latest. I’ve never had an alarm; I’ve always been an early riser. I have my first cup of coffee in bed. I watch the news. My wife and I often take a walk in the morning; we walk to
Clove Lakes Park
if the weather is good.
PASTA SPECIAL
It’s a big breakfast day. If I have leftover spaghetti, I make a spaghetti omelet. I cook it slow and long until it’s crispy on the outside. I always offer it to Nina and the girls. I say, ‘Hey girls, want some spaghetti omelet,’ and they say, ‘No way.’ They make fun of me.
CULTIVATING THE GARDEN
I love to play guitar in the morning, then it’s off to the garden. It goes from weeding into a project. I have a little O.C.D., a little A.D.D. I could go in the garage and see a tool and it leads to a project.
SINGING PRAISE
Nina and I are in the church choir at
Blessed Sacrament
. Typically, we sing at the 11 a.m. Mass, but it’s off for the summer. The choir is quite talented. I only joined a year ago, but my wife’s been there many years.
GEARING UP
If there is no plan for an outing, around 11, I will start packing for an upcoming sand job. I like to get that out of the way. For an upcoming trip, I have a list of things I need for work. I pack a water sprayer, hoses, shovels, carving tools, kneepads, a wheelbarrow to get your stuff from the road to beach site. Once you are on the beach, you really don’t want to have to leave.
BRONX BOUND
A favorite local day trip is the
New York Botanical Garden
and lunch on
Arthur Avenue
. At the gardens, they always have something different. So many flowers have such a short season so it doesn’t matter when you go there, you’ll always see something different. Then we go to
Zero Otto Nove
on Arthur Avenue. I like listening to the specials, and I like to experiment a little. My wife is a great cook. She’s Sicilian, so I’ve had all the common Italian dishes as well as they can be done, so when I get there I like to have something a little different.
TINKER TIME
We are usually back by midafternoon, so it’s typically projects around the house. I don’t sit still well, so I’m always occupied. I go into the garage. I’m working on a new water element, a little fountain. I built all the decks myself. Days off exhaust me because I rarely stop doing something.
FAMILY DINNER
My day doesn’t wrap up until 5 or 6. We share the cooking duties. We’ve always eaten dinner together. We do barbecue a lot in the summer on the deck. If we are cooking together, I’m cutting vegetables. She’s marinating the meat. I mostly handle the grilling. By the end of the summer, we just want it to cool off so we can have a roast or a bowl of chili. She creates marinades so the stuff isn’t plain and simple. We throw meatloaf sometimes on the grill. My kids are hardly spoiled but as far as living in the house, they are kind of like living in an all-inclusive hotel — minus the maid service.
ARMCHAIR THRILLERS
We D.V.R. everything so we don’t have to deal with commercials. We enjoyed “
Elementary
” quite a bit. We are, like the rest of America, waiting for “
Homeland
” to kick up again. We’ve been watching “
24
.” It’s good stuff. It’s one or two shows a night and then I read until I fall asleep.
EARLY TO BED
Lights out is anywhere between 10 and 11. That’s why we record a lot of shows. If you aren’t going to make it till 11, it’s best to record the show.

PLAINVIEW, Tex. —  They call this part of the world the giant side of Texas, just under the panhandle, where the crunchy brown fields and watercolor skies seem endless, with the occasional cluster of pine trees standing as conspicuously as skyscrapers.
From his perch thousands of feet in the air, Dr. Michael T. Graves had the best vantage point, traversing over open land and the tiny city with downtown streets paved in red brick. The long-winged aircraft he was piloting had a single propeller, but it wasn’t running. Instead, on this afternoon, he was using rising columns of warm air called thermals to lift him higher and higher.
Dr. Graves, 64, is the sole urologist covering an area of at least a half-dozen counties. His work can be sedentary and stressful. Some days, he spends hours in the operating room. To counteract that and to burn off energy, he rides motorcycles and swims and soars, taking part in the sport of using sailplanes, often without engines, to fly.
Soaring is a sport in that it has contests with competitors pushing to go faster and farther. Yet for many participants, the pursuit is less about the thrill of victory and more about the magical sensation of taking to the air like a bird, with the roar of the wind whipping past them.
The sailplanes, or gliders, they fly are more gangly and lightweight than the typical airplane. Some, like Dr. Graves’, have an engine to help them taxi to the runway and get off the ground; others need to be towed by another plane to get aloft. In soaring, pilots rely on natural forces to navigate, usually bouncing from one thermal column to another to stay in the air for hours, with the best pilots soaring 600 miles or more. Unlike hang gliding, fliers are ensconced in a bubble of a cockpit like the ones on a fighter jet.
“It’s probably the ultimate sport,” Dr. Graves said. “It requires a modicum of fitness, judgment, alertness.” And as he flies, he said, he feels a state of “serenity like you’d accomplish in a successful meditation.”
Dr. Graves, who discovered soaring in 2004, has owned planes for much of his adult life. As a young doctor in Iowa, he would fly himself home to California for Thanksgiving, stopping off for fuel and candy bars. In the years since, he said, he had flown left-front seat — the main pilot’s chair — over every continent but Antarctica, even island hopping across the Pacific to make his way to Australia.
“None of that,” he said, “was a challenge at all compared to an hour in a glider, just staying aloft.”
The terrain here in Texas, so flat and vast, lends itself to soaring. There is always a clear pasture to land in. And open countryside, plowed fields in particular, are quick to absorb the sun’s heat, making them especially conducive to thermal updrafts that pilots circle like a hawk to propel themselves higher and farther. “Doing that, you can get from here to Nebraska,” said Dr. Graves, who, on one trip from Brownfield, Tex., managed to reach Ulysses, Kan., about 340 miles north.
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
But soaring stretches far beyond these plains, with enthusiasts flying — and competing — around the world and with dozens of chapters of the
Soaring Society of America
scattered from coast to coast. Pilots can find thermals in the desert, even above an asphalt parking lot. The planes can also be guided by other natural forces, such as so-called mountain waves, which are created when strong winds run perpendicular to ridges.
The society, created in 1932, has about 11,000 members, with pilots as young as 14 eligible to fly. But the sport tends to skew much older, stoking some fear that it might be a fading pastime. The average age is about 60, and it is mostly men who have the time and money for a sport that can demand a fair share of both. (Used, low-end soaring planes start at about $10,000, and high-end new ones can cost as much as $250,000.)
“We’re getting longer and longer in the tooth,” said Bill Hill, 72, who has been flying sailplanes for over 50 years, “but there are not the people coming in at the bottom to take the place of geezers like myself.”
Mr. Hill, a retired commercial airline pilot in Cedar Crest, N.M., and others hope to sell soaring to younger pilots, especially those who fly professionally.
“Flying gliders, compared to airplanes, is like chess to checkers,” said Burt Compton, a flight instructor in Marfa, Tex., who learned to fly sailplanes from his father.
On a recent afternoon, Dr. Graves tugged open the bulky sliding doors of the hangar at the Hale County airport that held a few single- and double-engine planes and his touring glider, which, in comparison, looked like a lanky basketball player in a crowd. The wingspan of his Brazilian-built aircraft, called a Super Ximango, stretches 60 feet.
He started washing down the glider’s spindly appendages and windshield, preparing for takeoff. He checked a briefing from the Federal Aviation Administration, as well as the atmospheric conditions, which made for a lovely day but were not quite right for the thermals that could push him to the upper reaches where gliders are permitted to fly.
The puny engine on Dr. Graves’ aircraft, however, sounded like a neighbor mowing a lawn at the far end of the street.
“You see how slow this puppy climbs?” Dr. Graves said. “It’s only 81 horses. It’s less than some of my motorcycles.”
But it did its job, lifting him and a student pilot off the ground and allowing the glider to shrink against the giant blue sky. Once they had ascended a few thousand feet, Dr. Graves cut off the engine, leaving the willowy aircraft to be guided by the wind and the surgeon’s steady hand.

WASHINGTON — President Obama is nominating Gen. Joseph F. Dunford Jr., the commander of American and allied forces in Afghanistan, to lead the Marine Corps as commandant, the Defense Department said Thursday.
General Dunford, if confirmed by the Senate, would succeed Gen. James F. Amos, who is retiring, as the Marine Corps’ top officer and a member of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
General Dunford is a Boston native and a combat veteran who led a regiment in the 2003 invasion of Iraq. He would take over a Marine Corps that is making a transition from a focus on ground combat in Iraq and Afghanistan to its more traditional emphasis on rapid-strike amphibious operations.
He is highly regarded across the Marine Corps, where he is viewed as possessing not only battlefield and command experience, but also the ability to explain the military’s mission to the American public and Congress.
General Dunford faces the challenge of integrating female Marines into combat after the former secretary of defense, Leon E. Panetta,
lifted a ban on women serving in such roles
early last year.
General Dunford took over as commander in Afghanistan early last year to
manage the withdrawal
of the roughly 68,000 American troops who were still there and to ensure that Afghan forces were prepared to take over security from them.
About 32,000 American troops are still in the country. Last week, Mr. Obama said that he
planned to withdraw
the last troops by the end of 2016, with levels dropping to 9,800 after this year.
In a statement, General Amos said he was “extremely pleased” with the president’s selection of General Dunford.
“Joe is one of the most knowledgeable and talented leaders and thinkers in the military today,” he said. He said that General Dunford’s command of allied forces in Afghanistan over the last 18 months had been “extraordinary, and is testament to the full measure of the man.”
“Our country and our Marine Corps will benefit greatly from his continued service,” he continued.
General Dunford has a master’s degree in government from Georgetown University and a master’s in international relations from the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy at Tufts University.
The Marines took the brunt of some of the bloodiest battles of the last decade, most notably the November 2004 battle in Falluja, Iraq, in which dozens of Marines were killed and many more were wounded. It was considered the corps’ biggest fight since Vietnam. The reclaiming of the city by insurgents early this year
stunned
many of the Marines who had fought there.

One of the few certainties in the music business these days is that if
Taylor Swift
puts out a new album, it will sell by the truckload.
Her last two records, “Red” and “Speak Now,” each sold more than one million copies in its first week out, an increasingly rare feat as music sales weaken, and listening habits shift to online streaming services like Spotify and YouTube. Two years ago, “Red” started with 1.2 million sales, the
biggest opening in a decade
and the last time that any album has crossed the million mark in one week.
But the fate of Ms. Swift’s newest release, “1989,” which comes out Monday, has been the subject of nervous speculation in the industry for months, given not only the poor sales climate over all but also Ms. Swift’s decision to break from country radio, a vital source of support since the beginning of her career.
This year, no new title has cracked the one-million-sales mark — a symbolic milestone — and album sales over all are down 14 percent from the same period last year. According to Billboard magazine, “1989” is projected to sell at least 800,000 copies in its debut week.
In August, Ms. Swift, who was born in 1989, announced the release of “1989” through a fan gathering at the
Empire State Building
that was streamed live by Yahoo, the first volley in a steady and
aggressive marketing campaign
. She called the release her “very first documented, official pop album.”
It was the culmination of a long transition in her music toward pop and came as little surprise to her fans or the industry at large. But the break with country was definitive. The first single, “Shake It Off,” was a hit on Top 40 radio and went straight to No. 1, yet it was largely ignored by country programmers. While Ms. Swift’s record company, Big Machine, had sent country stations special remixes of some of her earlier pop-leaning songs, no such effort was made with “Shake It Off.”
“A lot of folks wished that she would have done some songs that would be more compatible with country radio, but she hasn’t,” said Joel Raab, a longtime consultant to country radio stations.
In the small world that is the Nashville music business, little outright negativity about Ms. Swift has been voiced publicly. A more prevailing sentiment is wistful pride.
“Taylor is one of us, one of our children,” said Mark Razz, the music director at WXTU-FM, a country station in Philadelphia. “You’re there for them along the way, and then they need to go to what they are going to do. She’s gotten to where she is through country music, and if she goes on to be the next pop sensation around the world, we are behind her 100 percent.”
Less support from country stations — now the
most popular music format
on radio — may hurt Ms. Swift’s sales. But her marketing campaign is intended to promote her as widely as possible, through brand tie-ins and a barrage on social media. Her
Diet Coke commercial
, for example, ends with a pitch for the album, and on Tuesday, Ms. Swift introduced a new song, “Style,” through a Target ad. Her Instagram feed has been a constant drumbeat of lyrics, images and hints related to the album.
The biggest hurdle for the success of “1989” may simply be the slumping world of music retail, with downloads now joining CDs as a declining format. Spotify and other streaming services, while growing in popularity, are not tracked in the same way as sales, and so far, the revenue those outlets generate has not made up for the drop in the number of albums sold.
Even if “1989” sells only 800,000 copies in its first week, that would more than double the next-biggest showing of the year, when Coldplay sold 383,000 copies of “Ghost Stories” in May. Big albums are expected later this year by One Direction, Lil Wayne and Kendrick Lamar, but Ms. Swift’s release is expected to be the most popular by far.
“It’s just very difficult to convince people to buy music,” said Keith Caulfield, an associate director of charts at Billboard. But if anyone can exceed expectations, Mr. Caulfield said, it is Ms. Swift.
“Forecasts are forecasts,” he added. “The weather changes.”

The latest round of labor market data released Friday add to an emerging puzzle whose resolution will be central to the future of the recovery.
We learned that employment is growing at a healthy clip, with 248,000 jobs created this month, and an average of 220,000 jobs created each month over the past year. Moreover, unemployment has fallen both further and faster than most had anticipated. The latest reading suggests that unemployment is down to 5.9 percent, and has fallen about a full percentage point in each of the past three years. These are all symptoms of a healthy economic expansion.
Normally, this would lead to faster wage growth. When workers feel their jobs are secure, they’re better positioned to ask for a raise. Likewise, when there are fewer people unemployed, companies need to pay better wages in order to attract talented workers.
Yet average hourly wages in the private sector were roughly flat in September (they fell by a penny), and they’ve grown at a rate of only around 2 percent over the past year. Alternative indicators also suggest that wage growth remains subdued.
This puzzle isn’t entirely new, as the usual link between unemployment and the rate of wage growth has totally broken down over recent years.
​
The recent data have made a sharp departure from the usual textbook analysis in which a tighter labor market leads to faster wage growth, and subsequent cost pressures feed through to higher inflation. Even as the recession threw millions of people out of work, wage growth barely slowed despite the textbook prediction to the contrary. Then through the ensuing recovery, unemployment fell rapidly, but again, wage growth has barely moved.
By the usual analysis, the key variable is how much “slack” there is in the labor market. When unemployment gets too low — toward what economists call the “natural rate” (don’t be fooled, there’s nothing natural about it) — there’s no more slack, and inflationary pressures start to build. This is the key reason the Federal Reserve has historically been nervous about keeping its foot pressed on the accelerator when unemployment got this low.
The problem is that economists don’t actually know how much slack there is in the economy, because we don’t know what unemployment rate the economy can sustain without sparking inflationary pressures. The Fed’s current
guess
is that the natural rate is around 5¼ or 5½ percent, although really, this is just a guess based on historical patterns. But it’s a critically important guess, because while unemployment’s not yet that low, the current trajectory puts us there soon. Indeed, this is the key reason the Federal Reserve policy makers have been talking about raising interest rates.
Given how starkly the latest episode has deviated from historical patterns, the wisdom of relying on past patterns repeating themselves seems questionable.
Indeed, the lack of any wage pressure right now stands starkly at odds with the view that the economy is about to run out of
slack
. Two explanations spring to mind. Perhaps the unemployment rate is giving us a false signal, and there are millions more workers waiting to return to the labor market than suggested by the official statistics. That is, the jobless will return when the jobs return. Or perhaps the natural rate is really much lower than most economists estimate. After all, at the end of the Clinton administration, unemployment was below 4 percent, while inflation remained low and stable.

Rather than guessing whether the labor market has run out of slack, why not look for more direct evidence? Perhaps we should be using current rates of wage growth to infer whether the economy is nearly out of slack. By this view, the expansion has still got quite a way to run.
To get a sense for this, realize that businesses will feel the need to start raising prices faster only if wage growth starts to exceed the rate of inflation, plus the rate of productivity growth. Given that the Fed is targeting inflation of 2 percent, and productivity typically grows at 1 to 2 percent, this suggests we should infer that the economy is about out of slack only when wage growth hits 3 to 4 percent.
The fact that the labor market isn’t delivering wage growth anywhere near this danger zone suggests that there remains a lot of slack left in the economy.
While many workers are no doubt frustrated that they’re not seeing wage gains, there’s a sunnier implication in all this for the jobless. Subdued wage growth is telling policy makers it would be premature to hang the “mission accomplished” banner above this recovery. We can do a lot better than an economy in which 9.3 million people remain unemployed.

In many places, waterfront dining conjures images of beachfront spots and vast expanses of water. On Long Island it often means a deck on a canal, as it does at Reel in East Rockaway.
For years this spot was the Fishery, which was damaged by
Hurricane Sandy
and subsequently bought by Shaun Manning and Lou Matarazzo, who was previously an owner of Edison’s Ale House in Manhasset and the Barefoot Peddler in Greenvale.
Last summer, while a renovation was still going on, they ran the restaurant under its old name. In November, when the work was completed and a new menu was in place, they
renamed it Reel
.
Reel is all about outdoor dining. Its deck seats 250, compared with 100 inside. On my visits, with temperatures in the 50s, there were a few hardy souls outside, but the indoor dining rooms were where the action was. Come summer, there will be live bands on the deck every night.
Inside, diners have a choice of two rooms. One has windows on three sides, with sea creatures and nautical symbols painted on the fourth wall and the ceiling. Floors are tiny white tiles throughout the restaurant; tables are bare; napkins are paper. With all the hard surfaces, the noise level is high.
A second, smaller dining room, with four to six tables, is a bit quieter, at least until the adjacent bar crowd breaks into full cry. It is windowless, with sea-blue walls and a painted shark on the ceiling as well as elsewhere around the room. We ended up calling it the shark tank.
The chef at Reel is
Adam Goldgell
, who previously cooked at
Sugo
in Long Beach and Panama Hattie’s in South Huntington, which has closed. Mr. Goldgell is a talented chef — he has appeared on the Food Network’s shows “Chopped” and “Restaurant Express” — and many of the dishes coming from his kitchen are noteworthy, but there was at least one dud in every course.
At the beginning of the meal, that dud was the under-seasoned and gloppy New England clam chowder. A crab-and-corn chowder special was marginally better but not memorable. We fared better with other appetizers, especially a mound of tuna tartare topped with an avocado half and with preserved-lemon aioli on the plate. Popcorn shrimp were lightly breaded and addictive, accompanied by a spicy cayenne mayonnaise. The shrimp cocktail of six firm, sweet jumbos for $12 was a bargain.
Be sure to check out the entree specials. One evening our favorite dish was from that list: roasted day boat cod atop a mix of maitake and shiitake mushrooms in a roasted-onion sauce. A delicious fried lobster ravioli, crisp outside, creamy within, was a worthy accompaniment.
Fish and chips and fried shrimp were good examples of those classics. The shrimp, though not bready, had a crisp coating that was a bit thicker than the ethereal ones I prefer. I would give it a B. Both fried seafood dishes came with good, skins-on French fries, creamy coleslaw and an ear of corn that was surprisingly sweet for this time of year. Those who prefer seafood broiled will like the broiled combo of hake fillets, oysters, scallops and shrimp in a garlic white wine sauce, with rice and mixed vegetables on the plate.
The dud among the entrees was the warm lobster roll, a favorite of mine. Alas, Reel’s version was dry and tasteless. The Reel burger, on the other hand, was a winner — thick, juicy and cooked precisely to order. It arrived under pimento cheese, caramelized onions and the sweet-salty crunch of candied bacon. Both sandwiches came with coleslaw and fries; other entrees included a respectable house salad.
The strikeout at dessert time was a warm blackberry cobbler under vanilla ice cream. The thick, doughy topper tasted strongly of baking soda and overwhelmed the scant layer of berries. We liked a strawberry pudding studded with strawberries and blackberries with a sprinkle of crisp phyllo strips. Its rubbery meringue topknot was easily pushed aside. Key lime pie was what it should be: creamy and tangy.
Reel is bound to heat up the South Shore dining scene this summer. With careful choosing, patrons can eat well there.

To the Editor:
Re “
The Piecemeal Assault on Health Care
” (editorial, Nov. 23):
The American people aren’t the only ones who will suffer from the systematic dismantling of the Affordable Care Act. It’s also bad news for America’s hospitals.
The health law’s hospital cuts — a staggering $245 billion over the first 14 years — include enormous cuts to the special Medicare and Medicaid payments hospitals receive for caring for uninsured and low-income patients. These “disproportionate share” funds were cut on the theory that insurance expansion would reduce the need for hospitals to provide uncompensated care.
That theory was strained at best, and never included the undocumented, uninsured immigrants who will continue to flood hospital emergency rooms for their care — and they won’t be turned away.
Despite these flaws, the hospital community continues to support the law’s promise of extending health insurance to tens of millions of uninsured Americans. That’s why the very real threat of the law’s unraveling is so troubling.
Not only could millions of newly insured Americans lose their coverage, but hospitals — the indispensable safety net for the country’s poor and uninsured — would also still be on the hook for hundreds of billions in funding cuts. That’s a lose-lose situation.
KENNETH E. RASKE
President, Greater New York
Hospital Association
New York, Nov. 24, 2014

Licia Albanese, an Italian-born soprano whose veneration by audiences worldwide was copious even by the standards of operatic adulation, died on Friday at her home in Manhattan. She was 105.
Her son, Joseph Gimma, confirmed her death.
After making her debut in Europe in the 1930s, Miss Albanese (her name is pronounced LEECH-ya al-buh-NAY-zay) went on to become one of the most admired sopranos of the mid-20th century. She had a long association with the
Metropolitan Opera
in New York, where she sang in more than 400 productions from 1940 to 1966.
Miss Albanese was what is called a lirico-spinto soprano, with a voice suited both for lyric roles and for somewhat weightier fare. A Puccini specialist, she was known in particular for the title role in “Madama Butterfly,” a part she sang more than 300 times. Her other notable Puccini roles included Mimi in “La Bohème,” the title part in “Tosca” and Liù in “Turandot.”
She was also famous as Violetta in Verdi’s “La Traviata,” singing the role nearly 90 times with the Met, a company record to this day. Writing in The New York Herald Tribune in December 1942, the composer and critic Virgil Thomson reviewed Miss Albanese’s first Violetta:
“She used her limpid voice, her delicate person and her excellent musicianship to equal effect in creating the character,” he wrote, adding, “I use the word ‘create’ for her achievement because that is what she really did.”
By virtue of longevity, Miss Albanese was very likely the last singer of her generation to have been considered a prima donna assoluta — a prima donna so exalted that she exceeds nearly all others in esteem.
Her voice was not large, nor, in the opinion of critics, was it unusually beautiful. But what her lower register may have lacked in luster, her soaring top range, with its silvery sheen, more than made up for.
Miss Albanese onstage was a sight to behold. Known for her sensitive dramatic interpretations, her nuanced physical gesture, her pinpoint diction in a number of languages and the passionate intensity she brought to singing and acting, she seemed to inhabit her characters — in particular Puccini’s doomed, fragile heroines — more fully than almost any other singer.
Her deep preparation for her roles included, for the consumptives Mimi and Violetta, visiting a tuberculosis ward — no small risk for one whose livelihood depended on breath.
Rehearsing Cio-Cio-San, the tragic heroine of “Madama Butterfly,” she realized that Puccini had not left sufficient pause in the music so that the character might easily take off her shoes before entering a house, in the traditional Japanese manner. Miss Albanese took her stage shoes home with her, slipping them off again and again until she could do it with all due speed.
She was said to have a special talent for mortality. As the “International Dictionary of Opera” said:
“Nowhere was Albanese’s mastery of her art more palpable than during the moments that required her to ‘expire’ onstage, something she invariably accomplished with the most exquisite expressivity, whether called upon to demonstrate a gradual, quiet fading away (Mimi, ‘La Bohème’); a final feverish outburst (Violetta, ‘La Traviata’); an intense losing battle to cheat death (Manon Lescaut); or an act of unbearable poignancy such as the suicide of Butterfly.”
Continue reading the main story
This approach to the art of sung drama won Miss Albanese rapturous adoration. She spent her prime awash in bouquets at curtain calls, as audience members chanted her name in unison. A coterie of her most hard-core admirers spent years traveling from city to city like camp followers just to hear her perform.
Yet she was no diva, by all accounts displaying little of the personal affectation that can come with the territory.
“Diva? Hah! I was never a diva,” Miss Albanese told The San Francisco Chronicle in 2004. “Only God makes a diva. No, just call me a plain singer with lots of expression.”
Because she knew better than to attempt heavy works, like Wagner, which can erode the voice over time, Miss Albanese was able to keep singing well into old age. Long after her official retirement, she was heard for decades on every Met opening night at
Lincoln Center
, her voice ringing ceremonially out from her box with “The Star-Spangled Banner,” including an impeccable high B flat.
In 1985, Miss Albanese sang the role of the aging diva Heidi Schiller in a highly regarded concert version of Stephen Sondheim’s musical “Follies” with the New York Philharmonic. That production, which also starred Carol Burnett, Barbara Cook, Elaine Stritch and Mandy Patinkin, is available in a live recording.
Her many other recordings include a celebrated “La Bohème,” made in 1946 to commemorate the opera’s 50th anniversary, under the baton of Arturo Toscanini, a frequent collaborator.
Miss Albanese also collaborated with some of the most eminent male singers of her time, whose names evoke a grand bygone era. Among them were Jan Peerce, with whom she partnered many times at the Met, and Ezio Pinza, a notorious trickster who made one of her swan songs even more difficult than normal:
“I remember a ‘Bohème’ broadcast when I kept smelling something terrible in the final scene, where I was dying,” Miss Albanese told The New York Times in 1989. “I kept singing, but in between I would whisper to everyone, ‘My God, what is that smell?’ And finally at the end, Pinza pulled a herring out from under my pillow.”
Felicia Albanese was born in Bari, in southern Italy, on July 23, 1909. She began singing as a girl, becoming a pupil of Giuseppina Baldassarre-Tedeschi, a noted Butterfly in her day.
Miss Albanese made her debut unexpectedly in 1934, at the Teatro Lirico in Milan. At a performance of “Madama Butterfly” at which she was understudying the title role, the soprano became ill during Act I. Miss Albanese was hustled onstage for Act II.
A great success, she went on to appear at La Scala, Covent Garden and other European houses.
She left Italy for New York in 1939 and the next year, on Feb. 9, made her Met debut as Cio-Cio-San. Reviewing her performance in The Times, Olin Downes wrote:
“She sounded the note of tragedy and made it the more poignant by the constant light and shade of her dramatic interpretation. There was a real simplicity and contagious emotion in it, and everything was so thoughtfully proportioned that climaxes had never to be forced or passion torn to tatters to make it carry across the footlights.”
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
At the Met, Miss Albanese’s other roles included Susanna in Mozart’s “Marriage of Figaro,” Micaela in Bizet’s “Carmen,” Marguerite in Gounod’s “Faust” and Desdemona in Verdi’s “Otello.” She was also a mainstay at the San Francisco Opera, where she sang for many years.
Miss Albanese, who became a United States citizen in the 1940s, received the National Medal of Arts from President Bill Clinton in 1995.
In retirement, Miss Albanese gave master classes around the world. In 1974 she and her husband, Joseph A. Gimma, established the Licia Albanese-Puccini Foundation, which aids up-and-coming singers.
Mr. Gimma, a Wall Street broker and a former chairman of the New York State Racing Commission whom Miss Albanese married in 1945, died in 1990. Besides her son, her survivors include two grandchildren and three great-grandchildren.
In September 1966, when the Metropolitan Opera moved from its storied old home at 39th Street and Broadway to its new one at Lincoln Center, Miss Albanese did not come along: She had left the company shortly before in a dispute with the Met’s imperious general manager, Rudolf Bing, who she felt was underusing her.
The previous April, she had sung Cio-Cio-San’s aria “Un Bel Di” at the farewell gala at the old Met. At aria’s end, she knelt, kissed her hand and touched it to the stage.
After the opera house was torn down, The Times reported in 1997, Miss Albanese could be seen on some fine days standing amid the rubble, dressed, as if in mourning weeds, in her Butterfly kimono.
Correction: August 16, 2014
An earlier version of this article incorrectly characterized Ezio Pinza, a singer with whom Miss Albanese performed. He was a bass, not a tenor.

An influx of talented young dealers is creating a renaissance at the Puces, Paris’s historic flea market.
Paris’s
Marché aux Puces de Saint-Ouen
, said to be the world’s largest flea market, traces its origins back to the 19th-century ragpickers who used to congregate outside the city’s northern walls and sell their scavenged goods. Today, things are a little more professional, and the stakes are higher. “I work like a gallerist,” Edouard Demachy says of his stand within
Marché Paul Bert Serpette
, the largest of the Puces’ 14 markets. At another stall, he once scored an extremely rare Gio Ponti majolica vase. “One of three in the world, the other two are in museums,” he says proudly. Demachy sold it to one of Italy’s most prominent Ponti collectors, who is currently creating a foundation where it will be shown.
Still in his 30s, Demachy is part of a new generation of sellers infusing youth and energy into Paul Bert Serpette. After nearly a decade of stagnation and legal troubles, the market has been quietly undergoing a revival over the last couple of years, a trend that was underscored last spring when the French media entrepreneur Jean-Cyrille Boutmy bought it from the Duke of Westminster, who sold it at an estimated $27 million loss. Since taking over, Boutmy has been praised for both preserving the historic legacy of the market and attempting to modernize it. In addition to implementing strict measures designed to ensure the quality and provenance of the market’s wares, Boutmy plans to repaint the facade of Serpette, the market’s indoor space, and to build on initiatives like the Philippe Starck-designed restaurant Ma Cocotte, which opened in 2012. Boutmy is also appealing to a new crop of savvy young dealers with the planned redesign of the Paul Bert Serpette website. These changes are already having an effect — 50 new dealers have opened shop during the last two years, and many of them are under 40.
The Puces has always been a proving ground for young dealers, and several of the newcomers are second- or third-generation sellers, already armed with the sophistication and knowledge required to mount displays as polished as those in the shops in Saint-Germain-des-Prés or the Marais. Before opening his Serpette stand, dedicated to rare 20th-century French ceramics and postwar French and Italian furniture, Demachy ran the 20th-century department of his father’s prestigious gallery, Camoin Demachy. One of the market’s youngest vendors, 23-year-old Hugo Greiner runs a stall in Serpette as an offshoot of his mother’s three Left Bank galleries, where he sells mainly midcentury pieces, such as lighting by the American artists Mark Weinstein and C. Jeré.
Aurélien Jeauneau is another example of this new kind of merchant. Though only 28, Jeauneau opened his Paul Bert stand last fall with nearly two decades of exposure to antiquing. The son of a dealer, he began prowling secondhand markets at the age of 8, and when he was 15, brought home a Pierre Paulin Mushroom chair he found on the sidewalk on his way home from school. Today, Jeauneau’s stand focuses on the industrial furniture of the French designer Pierre Guariche from the 1950s and 1960s. “He made beautiful things for the price of ugly ones,” Jeauneau explains, pointing to a streamlined cabinet with a drop desk. “There isn’t one design that doesn’t work, and yet eight out of 10 clients don’t know him.”

The expertise and enthusiasm among these legacy dealers is also attracting outsiders to the trade. The 29-year-old Maxime Ramond-Bluzet, who deals in vintage French luxury goods from the early 20th century, moved into Paul Bert last October. Though he doesn’t have any family ties to antiquing, his interest in collecting was sparked at age 17 when he purchased his first piece of furniture — a Napoleon III games table. Another recent convert is 26-year-old Archibald Pearson, whose great-uncle is a former president of France and whose mother is a top Parisian publicist and event organizer. After apprenticing with another dealer for six months, Pearson established his place in the community in 2012 when he took over Paul Bert’s largest plot and, last May, invited three neighboring dealers, Frédéric Ozier, Thomas Tardif and Emmanuel Renoult, to join him there. “We’re like a village,” he says of his friends and associates. “People are welcoming. If you’re absent, neighbors will ring you.” Since Boutmy took over, problems are addressed quickly, which has created an atmosphere of good will between dealers. Pearson, Ozier, Tardif and Renoult sell to each other and occasionally even acquire large items as a team, such as a pair of bronze-trimmed, leather-topped 1940s wooden library tables from the legendary decorating house Jansen.
This kind of camaraderie has made young dealers reluctant to consider working anywhere else. “In Paris now, unless you have a gallery full of Picassos and need to be on the Left Bank, Paul Bert Serpette is the best place to be,” says Marion Attanasio, a bubbly 25-year-old who spends her weekdays working on her art history master’s thesis and her weekends selling 19th-century portraits and landscapes. That feeling is echoed by many of the young dealers, who see in the Puces the opportunity to learn while establishing themselves in the field. “It’s the best school,” Attanasio says. “To work here is to see marvelous objects every day.”

The Agenda
How small-business issues are shaping politics and policy.
Last month, in a
discussion
about how raising the minimum wage might affect small companies, we noted that there could be more empathy among elected officials for how entrepreneurs manage their businesses. Inspired by the
suggestion
that members of Congress ought to try managing a small business for a week, we invited small-business owners who were willing to open their doors to an elected official for a day to let us know by email.
Two business owners did.
In Oregon, Eric Miller, who owns
Squishymedia
, a website developer for nonprofits and government agencies, acknowledged that his 14 employees would not be directly affected by increasing the minimum wage. But he said that for the kind of sites he builds, which often present complex data to the general public, growing income inequality hurt his business. (Squishymedia’s annual revenue exceeds $1 million a year.) “We strive to make our work as accessible as possible to broad audiences,” he wrote in an email, “but the reality is that not all audiences are in the best position to take advantage of what we’re trying to offer. These are complex issues and topics. And just as there’s a growing economic gap within American society, there’s a growing digital skills gap, and our economic and educational policies are exacerbating that issue.”
In addition to the direct financial benefits, Mr. Miller continued, raising the minimum wage will free low-wage earners up to do other important things. “Someone who has to work 60-plus hours a week at three jobs isn’t going to be able to finish a degree program or read to their kids,” he wrote. “If we’re going to be competitive as individuals and as a nation, we need to invest in our people.”
In North Carolina, which could determine which party controls the Senate, Katrina Ryan employs 30 people in the summer and 50 during the school year at two bakeries and desert cafes known as
Sugarland
, a bustling purveyor of “caffeine, sugar and alcohol” with annual revenue of just under $2 million. “We are in the minor vice business,” said Ms. Ryan, who began her email by illustrating how raising the minimum wage would affect far more employees than those making it now. Here is her note:
I am a small business owner, in the dreaded “food service” industry, and I’m pretty liberal. I work very hard to pay everyone that works for me more than minimum wage by a good bit, and across the board, we have always paid for 100 percent of our full-time employees health insurance, we have paid leave and sick time, none of which is required or even common in North Carolina. Still, I’m pretty frosted about this. By paying more, I am able to hire better workers than the average minimum wage worker, and so, of course, my wages will have to go up, and since I already commit 46 percent of my gross revenue to payroll, it means that some things for my higher paid employees will have to go. There just isn’t more payroll in the budget.
We see a lot of people who try to get jobs here that we would never hire for any wage, ever. They can’t spell the word bakery on an application. They can’t provide a phone number to call them back in for an interview, There are just other issues that have nothing to do with the cost of labor. Invariably, when you do make an exception and try to give someone a chance, sooner (usually about three paychecks in) or later, they just don’t show up one busy weekend day. Sometimes it’s drugs, sometimes it’s jail, but I had one dishwasher have “deaths in the family” eight Saturdays in a single quarter. This is a guy we paid $9.50 an hour, which is crazy money in North Carolina. While I have compassion for people really trying to make ends meet, I have 30 or 40 other employees that I am responsible to, and it’s not fair to them to keep employees like this around. That’s who ends up in long-term minimum wage jobs, people with no skills and personal/social issues that keep them from being able to show up regularly to work.
Subsidized reliable day care would be a better investment than randomly upping the minimum wage. It would help mothers be more reliable employees, which would get them more opportunity. Mandatory basic job skills training courses, as in writing that isn’t in text code, and enough basic math to make change from a $20 for everyone collecting an unemployment check isn’t a bad idea either. How about fines for companies equal to 100 percent of the amount that their employees collect from public assistance programs to fund some initiatives to make those at the very bottom of the employment ladder a little more valuable in the labor market? Or even just some prepaid cell phones so they can schedule job interviews. I took a grand total of nine days off last year. My staff can tell you the number of times this year that they’ve come in at 6 or 7 a.m. and I’m still here from the day before. That’s what it takes to build and grow a small business in this environment. I don’t have extra money for wages. It’ll come straight out of my 401(k) and all of my employees who earn 30K to 50K, and at some point, if there’s not any revenue, there’s really not any point in working.
When I reached Ms. Ryan later and asked her what other issues she was most concerned about, she responded, “reining in for-profit colleges and not having every 27-year-old with $20,000 to $30,000 in debt.” Ms. Ryan said that these debts made it difficult to hire recent graduates from culinary schools. “One of the things I want to make sure is that employees can pay their bills,” she said, “because they’re better employees if they don’t have to work two jobs.”
She also complained about the complexities of state sales tax law. Food, she said, is taxed at one rate, and prepared food at another — and then there is, she said, an “
artisan bakery exemption
” to the prepared food tax. “Figuring out what rate to charge depends on whether you give them a fork or not,” she said. “A lot of it depends on which auditor is looking at your books and whether you paid the proper tax rate or not. The arbitrariness of these laws makes reporting obligations very stressful.”
There was more, much more. If you represent, or aspire to represent, the good citizens of either Oregon or North Carolina — perhaps you’re a candidate in a hotly contested Senate campaign and your name is
Kay Hagan
or
Thom Tillis
— and want to get to know your small-business constituency better, please write me at
robb.mandelbaum@nytimes.com
and I’ll connect you with Mr. Miller or Ms. Ryan.

., the federal appellate case discussed in the Op-Ed essay.

The Times has converted all of its 1964 issues into a digitized, searchable format. Each week, The Upshot will unearth an item from 50 years ago and put it in the light of today.
“
U.S. Negro Voters Put at 5.5 Million
” appeared on Oct. 13 and can be seen in its original format on
TimesMachine.
Weeks before the presidential election of 1964, African-Americans and their advocates were working toward a record turnout.
The
National Association for the Advancement of Colored People
announced that it had registered 5.5 million black voters in 34 states and the District of Columbia as of Oct. 1, and estimated that the black electorate could number as many as 12 million.
In the end, that was about how many blacks turned out, according to census data compiled after the fact: Turnout reached 58.5 percent for an estimated black population of 20.7 million. Data on voting by race isn’t available for years before 1964, but the N.A.A.C.P. estimated at the time that no more than 5 million African-Americans voted in the presidential election of 1960.
Black voters wouldn’t go to the polls at such levels again until President Obama’s first election in 2008, when 60.8 percent of them voted. In 2012, 62 percent turned out for Mr. Obama’s re-election.
What’s most impressive about the 1964 result, though, is that it happened at a time when some Southern states still viciously repressed blacks’ attempts to vote. That wouldn’t begin to end until the following year, when the
Voting Rights Act
passed with the strong support of President Lyndon B. Johnson, who owed much of his re-election margin to that enormous black turnout.
In fact, black turnout outside the South hit 72 percent in 1964, a level it has not reached since. In the South, black turnout was just 44 percent.
Those numbers would begin converging in 1968, and by the 1990s black turnout in the South was identical to the rates seen in the rest of the country. Southern black turnout even exceeded the rest of the country’s for President Obama’s two elections.
This does not necessarily portend anything for next month’s midterm elections. While the rate of black turnout will be critical in Georgia, as my colleague Nate Cohn
has written
, and possibly elsewhere, history offers little guidance here.
Black turnout in presidential years has been steadily increasing since 1996, but it has been generally flat in midterm years. Black turnout in 2010 was 40.7 percent, only one percentage point above its average since 1966.

Update: The New York Times
reported today
that a helicopter carrying correspondent Alissa Rubin and photographer Adam Ferguson crashed in Northern Iraq today. The pilot was killed and Ms. Rubin was injured.
“A helicopter carrying aid from Iraq’s Kurdish autonomous government to stranded Yazidi refugees in the Sinjar mountains of northern Iraq crashed on Tuesday, killing the pilot and injuring other passengers, including a New York Times journalist on assignment for the newspaper.
Alissa J. Rubin
, 56, The Times’s Paris bureau chief and a longtime war correspondent, suffered an apparent concussion and broken wrists but was conscious, she confirmed when contacted briefly by cellphone.
Adam Ferguson
, 35, a freelance photographer working for The Times who was accompanying her, said via cellphone that he was not injured.
The helicopter, which had delivered emergency aid and picked up some Yazidi evacuees, crashed shortly after it took off, survivors said.”
Moises Saman, a Magnum photographer, was also on the helicopter and was not seriously injured.
Over the last four days,
Adam Ferguson
has photographed members of Iraq’s Yazidi minority religious group who had been surrounded on a mountaintop without water or food as a result of battlefield advances made by Sunni militants. As the refugee crisis continues, some have been able to escape into Syria this weekend. Mr. Ferguson, 35, freelances extensively for The New York Times as well as for National Geographic and Time magazine, and he spoke to James Estrin on Monday morning by phone from northern Iraq. Their conversation has been edited.
Q.
Where are you?
A.
I’ve been in northern Iraq for the last three days. There were 30,000 to 40,000 people trapped on Sinjar mountain, surrounded by the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria, which has taken the villages in this area. It’s pretty dire.
Everyone’s been quite worried about them dying out there on the mountain. Kurdish militia groups teamed up with Yazidi volunteer fighters and they made it possible for many of the people that were stuck to escape.
Huge numbers of refugees started
fleeing across the border
into Syria and then around back east to Iraq. I saw a lot of people people coming across the border. On Saturday, we managed to
get right down to the river
, and there were thousands of people fleeing across the border. It was horrific. Many had lost family members in the mountains and watched people starve around them. They had been stuck in the mountains for six days. Groups of women were wailing as they walked across the border.
Q.
And they were Yazidi?
A.
The vast majority of them are Yazidi, who are being executed because of their religion. They were being forced to convert and the men were being killed anyway after converting. Women were being taken away by ISIS.
Q.
You were in Syria Sunday?
A.
I managed to walk across the river and the Kurdish P.Y.D. (Democratic Union Party) gave me permission to enter into their controlled area in Syria. I went about 80-90 km inside Syria to a town called Derek.
The people from the mountain were taken into refugee camps in Syria before they took some of them back into Iraq. I drove in a taxi that night and photographed these people who went through horror in the mountains. The people coming through the mountains are desperate and are coming across the border into Syria. Some are circling back into Iraq further along the border.
Q.
What’s the mood in Baghdad?
A.
The mood in Baghdad is tense. I think most Shia and Sunni are anxious about the possibility of ISIS coming in and taking Baghdad. If ISIS comes into Baghdad there will likely be civil war.
Nobody expected Mosul to fall, so anything is possible although the Shia militias have been mobilizing and I think they’re going to fight for Baghdad pretty hard if it comes down to it. In Baghdad, most people don’t want the hardcore brand of extremism that ISIS has brought to a third of the country already.
Q.
You’ve been in Iraq before.
A.
This is my third trip. I came here for the first time in 2012. I pushed to get an assignment here because I’ve been in Afghanistan a lot and I really wanted to understand Iraq and what would happen after the Americans left.
Q.
Is it different from the last two visits?
A.
It’s always been difficult to work here. It is the hardest place I have ever worked. There is essentially a civil war going on and you can’t photograph most of it. You can’t cover the fighting without losing your head. The Iraqi military rarely lets you photograph them and covering the Syria border is difficult. Covering ISIS is not possible.
Even if you get all the right permissions from the government, you can still get to places and you
will
be shut down. I have tried to cover some of the Shia groups but a lot of people felt let down by the international community and there was definitely a resentment toward the foreign media.
Q.
How do you avoid ISIS when the front line is moving so quickly?
A.
Most of the time I am far from ISIS, but it is a calculated risk. It’s very difficult to cover areas that are right near ISIS unless you go with the Kurdish pesh merga and even then, you can’t get right to the front lines. I went to a Christian town and saw artillery a kilometer away. A lot of the Christians in the town were fleeing when we were driving there. It was still okay for us to be there but the next day that town fell to ISIS.
Q.
Have you run into people who have encountered ISIS in their villages?
A.
A lot of the Christians fled before ISIS arrived and the people who didn’t get out in time have stayed and suffered.
Q.
Have you had any experiences in Iraq, Afghanistan or elsewhere that have compared to this?
A.
The only thing that would compare is in 2011, I went to Kenya and photographed the refugees who were fleeing famine and conflict in Somalia. People walked for days to arrive to this refugee camp.
But this week was something else. It seemed biblical. I was standing on that bridge and watching a river of people crossing with makeshift backpacks around their shoulders, carrying children. It was family after family. Some of the women were crying, some lost their husbands, some lost their fathers. The elderly and the young were particularly vulnerable in the mountains.
I’ve never seen anything like that. You feel inadequate standing there with a camera, witnessing this incredibly important event. It’s very hard to make pictures that truly show the horror that the people have been through. People have left their home, their livelihood, their accumulated wealth and then spent six days in the mountains watching their relatives and friends dying around them with no idea if they’ll survive.
When they entered the refugee camp in Syria a lot of people started crying partly in relief, but also from the trauma of losing so much, and perhaps never being able to
return home.

Robert Slater, a journalist and the author of more than two dozen books, including biographies of figures as diverse as the Israeli leader Golda Meir, the businessman Jack Welch and the billionaire and philanthropist George Soros, died on March 25 in Jerusalem. He was 70.
The cause was complications of the flu, his wife, Elinor Slater, said in an email.
Mr. Slater was born in Manhattan, but spent much of his life in Israel, moving there in 1971. He worked for about two years for United Press International before joining the Jerusalem bureau of Time magazine. He covered the country for Time for two tumultuous decades, and his reporting and the relationships he made led to biographies of some of Israel’s most prominent leaders, including
Yitzhak Rabin
, the former prime minister; Moshe Dayan, the military leader; and Ms. Meir, who was prime minister from 1969 to 1974.
For “Golda: The Uncrowned Queen of Israel,” published in 1981, Mr. Slater relied on scores of interviews with friends, relatives and colleagues of Ms. Meir. In the book, he reported that King Hussein of Jordan told Ms. Meir during a series of secret discussions that he regretted having attacked Israel in 1967 — “a historic mistake,” the king called it, according to Mr. Slater.
Even as Mr. Slater covered Israel, he began a productive sideline writing business books, often with extensive cooperation from his subjects. He wrote three books about Mr. Welch, the former chief executive of General Electric, including
“29 Leadership Secrets from Jack Welch.”
Mr. Slater was born on Oct. 1, 1943, in Manhattan, and grew up in South Orange, N.J. His father, Joseph, was a financial officer for a cable and copper company, and his mother, the former Gertrude Levy, was a homemaker. He received his bachelor’s degree in 1966 from the University of Pennsylvania and in 1967 received his master’s degree from the London School of Economics in international relations. He briefly worked at The Bucks County Courier Times in Pennsylvania before joining the Trenton bureau of United Press International in 1969.
His books were sometimes criticized for portraying their subjects too favorably.
Reviewing his 1997 biography
of Michael Ovitz,
“Ovitz: The Inside Story of Hollywood’s Most Controversial Power Broker,”
Bernard Weinraub wrote in The New York Times, “Mr. Slater either failed to interview anyone who had a harsh word to say about Mr. Ovitz — all he had to do was walk over to any lunchtime table at the Grill, an industry hangout, in Beverly Hills — or didn’t believe that his subject was flawed.”
Mr. Slater was also the author of
“Great Jews in Sports.”
He also wrote books with his wife, including
“Great Jewish Women”
and
“Great Jewish Men.”
In addition to his wife, the former Elinor Resnik; his survivors include their three children, Miriam Binyamini, Adam Slater and Rachel Slater; and seven grandchildren.
From 1987 to 1990, Mr. Slater led the
Foreign Press Association
in Israel, which represented foreign reporters in discussions with the government and the military.
In recent years, he wrote a column for The Jerusalem Report.

In the search for love, are straight men always looking for women who are better looking than they are, and straight women holding out for men who are richer? Or do they tend to pair up with partners who are more on their level? Recent research suggests the latter — and this may have larger implications for how we talk about love and marriage.
At The Atlantic, James Hamblin
reports
on a study published by the sociologist Elizabeth McClintock in the journal American Sociological Review. Its gist:
“The dominant force in mating is
matching
.
“What appears to be an exchange of beauty for socioeconomic status is often actually not an exchange, McClintock wrote, but a series of matched virtues. Economically successful women partner with economically successful men, and physically attractive women partner with physically attractive men.”
People don’t trade hotness for wealth, Ms. McClintock found, but rather tend to find partners about as hot or rich as they are. Previous research may have overstated the importance of trading because it failed to take into account the fact that men on average are richer than women, and women on average are hotter than men. Ms. McClintock tells Mr. Hamblin:
“Women spend a lot more time trying to look good than men do. That creates a lot of mess in this data. If you don’t take that into account then you actually see there’s a lot of these guys who are partnered with women who are better looking than them, which is just because, on average, women are better looking. Men are partnering ‘up’ in attractiveness. And men earn more than women — we’ve got that 70 percent
wage gap
— so women marry ‘up’ in income. You’ve got to take these things into account before concluding that women are trading beauty for money.”
Ms. McClintock also argues that the notion of women trading beauty for wealth “sets up this idea of marriage being mercenary, which doesn’t fit with our usual conception that we kind of like our spouse and we want someone that we get along with.” Many readers might prefer the spouse-you-like formulation to the one that assigns monetary value to a woman’s resemblance to a supermodel. However, the “idea of marriage being mercenary” — or at least highly market-driven — is extremely common.
In her famous/infamous 2008 Atlantic story “Marry Him,” Lori Gottlieb
questioned
her own choice not to enter matrimony with any of the men she dated in her 20s and 30s: “Wouldn’t it have been wiser to settle for a higher caliber of ‘not Mr. Right’ while my marital value was at its peak?” In her formulation, what women can hope to get for their physical attractiveness isn’t wealth so much as help conceiving and caring for kids. She writes:
“Those of us who choose not to settle in hopes of finding a soul mate later are almost like teenagers who believe they’re invulnerable to dying in a drunk-driving accident. We lose sight of our mortality. We forget that we, too, will age and become less alluring. And even if some men do find us engaging, and they’re ready to have a family, they’ll likely decide to marry someone younger with whom they can have their own biological children. Which is all the more reason to settle before settling is no longer an option.”
Mark Regnerus, a sociologist, took an economic view of relationships in a 2011 Slate article. Essentially, he
argued
that an abundance of attractive, accomplished women on college campuses, coupled with a dearth of similarly accomplished men, was skewing the market for sex, love and marriage. He wrote:
“If women were more fully in charge of how their relationships transpired, we’d be seeing, on average, more impressive wooing efforts, longer relationships, fewer premarital sexual partners, shorter cohabitations, and more marrying going on. Instead, according to the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (which collects data well into adulthood), none of these things is occurring. Not one. The terms of contemporary sexual relationships favor men and what they want in relationships, not just despite the fact that what they have to offer has diminished, but in part because of it. And it’s all thanks to supply and demand.”
And this February, the Austin Institute for the Study of Family and Culture, where Mr. Regnerus is a senior fellow, released a
video
titled “The Economics of Sex.” “Let’s think about sex as an exchange,” one of its narrators offers. The video then runs through many of the same arguments Mr. Regnerus made in his Slate piece, concluding that women could trade sex for marriage, except that too many men are able to get sex for free. The solution: “Economists say that collusion — women working together — would be the most rational way to elevate the market value of sex.”
The idea of marriage as an exchange of sex for commitment has inspired significant criticism. In a Jezebel
response
to the video, Lindy West objects to the notion “that it is my biological imperative to trap a complete stranger into a lifelong contract based entirely on how many diamonds he’s willing to buy me with.” And of the idea that men want sex and women want marriage so the two must always arrange a trade, she writes:
“Human lives are simply not so simple. I know, because I have one, and everyone I know has one, and right-wing lawmakers (the keepers of that narrative)
have them too
, and every single one of those lives is messy and complex and unpredictable.”
Ms. McClintock’s study didn’t look at the same exchange of sex for commitment that “The Economics of Sex” discusses. But, she argues, her research does imply that the search for a partner is less about swapping beauty for money and more about finding someone with whom you share some traits in common. In her paper’s concluding paragraph, she writes, “This article questions the preeminence of the market model of partner selection in sociological research.” For those who find that model an insufficient explanation for our complicated lives, a little questioning may be welcome.

MIAMI —  When Bill Clinton attended a recent campaign rally for his party’s candidate for governor here, he whipped up the crowd with keystone Democratic issues — higher wages, better-funded schools and affordable health care.
Standing next to Mr. Clinton, however, was no longtime Democratic stalwart but a former Republican governor, Charlie Crist, who in an earlier life had suggested that Mr. Clinton resign from office amid the impeachment scandal.
“He did not leave the Republican Party,” Mr. Clinton told the crowd, hailing Mr. Crist, who switched parties and is now a Democrat, as a common-sense moderate. “They left on a jet airplane moving as far to the right as they could get.”
In one of the nation’s closest, costliest and most-watched governor’s races, the Florida contest between Mr. Crist and the Republican incumbent, Rick Scott, requires voters to step through the looking glass.
Allegiances have been scrambled, diluted or reversed. Voters endure disorienting political maneuvers: Pick up the phone and listen to robocalls that use old recordings of Republican Charlie Crist taking positions now intended to hurt the Democrat Charlie Crist. And watch Mr. Scott, a conservative political neophyte who today is better attuned to the vagaries of politics, tap dance to and fro, but mostly toward the center, on spending, education and the environment.
The biggest role reversal may involve a question that could be key to the fate of several Republican governors who are seeking re-election in November: Who gets credit for an economy that is stronger than when Mr. Scott was elected in the Republican wave in 2010? Even as Republicans nationally blast the Obama administration’s economic record as a dismal failure, governors like Mr. Scott and Rick Snyder in Michigan are promoting the improving economy in their states.
Both parties see something else at stake beyond presiding over the nation’s fourth most populous state: control of the levers of state government before the 2016 presidential election.
Continue reading the main story
Less than two months before Election Day, the two men are virtually tied in polls, with Mr. Scott, who trailed Mr. Crist early on, now squeaking past him in some of them. A third candidate, Adrian Wyllie, a Libertarian, seems likely to siphon votes from both candidates.
In interviews and polls, voters have hardly been swooning for any candidate, seemingly casting about for the least unpalatable option.
This is true of Edith Biller, a longtime Clearwater resident, which is near Mr. Crist’s home turf in a quintessential swing county. A lifelong Democrat, Mrs. Biller, 87, said she would vote for Mr. Crist, even though she was not thrilled with him “because he is a bit of flip-flopper” and did not do much when he was governor from 2007-11.
“But I just, I just don’t like Scott at all,” she said, adding that she does not trust him and believes that he bought the election last time by spending $70 million of his own money on the campaign and has mismanaged the state. “He scares me a little bit.”
Continue reading the main story
Her daughter, Joanie Biller-Cauce, a less committed Democrat from Miami, said she would probably vote for Mr. Crist but asked herself, “Is it all about winning for him?” In the end, she added, she might not vote at all.
At a Scott rally at La Carreta, a Cuban restaurant in Miami, Olga Suarez, 77, said Republicans were bitter about Mr. Crist and called him a “lost cause.”
“Republican to Democrat — por favor,” Mrs. Suarez said. “He won’t do anything he says he’s going to do.”
The issues are important, too: Mr. Scott, 61, promotes Florida’s revitalized economy and his drive for $1 billion in tax cuts, along with more funds for schools. Mr. Crist, 58, pledges an increase in the minimum wage, lower insurance rates and a fight for women’s and gay rights. But the issues all too often disappear in the muck of the campaign.
“The race is extremely negative,” said Rod Smith, a former chairman of the Florida Democratic Party. “It used to be when I asked someone, they would say, ‘I’m voting for Jeb Bush’ or ‘for Lawton Chiles,’ ” referring to two former governors. “The answer now seems to be, ‘I’m not voting for Charlie Crist’ or ‘I’m not voting for Rick Scott.’ ”
Republicans agree. “The winner of this race will have a 19 percent approval rating and the loser 17 percent,” said John M. Stipanovich, a longtime Republican political consultant.
The antipathy for both candidates reflects, in part, the deepening malaise among voters around the country. But it is also a reaction to a bitter campaign awash in negative advertisements, outside groups with political agendas and seemingly bottomless reservoirs of cash.
Mr. Scott is expected to spend at least $100 million in the race — this time, none from his pocket — and Mr. Crist about half that amount. Mr. Scott’s war chest, and that of the state Republican Party, fortified him with an early advantage; he began to run political TV ads months ago, lifting him up in polls and dragging Mr. Crist down. At the same time, a record 49 Scott field offices have opened around the state. His campaign says volunteers have knocked on one million doors.
But the fact that Mr. Crist withstood the early attacks, winding up tied at the moment, is a testament to his strength as a campaigner, political analysts on both sides said.
“What you are seeing,” said Steven A. Geller, a former Democratic state senator and Crist supporter, “is Charlie Crist being tough enough to absorb months-worth of body blows that would have knocked anybody else out.”
That is true, analysts said, but negative ads have a way of tamping down turnout in an off-year election, particularly among Democrats.
“A lot of their effort is designed to try to drive down turnout,” Steve Schale, an adviser to Mr. Crist who ran President Obama’s 2008 Florida campaign, said of the Scott campaign.
The ads cut to the heart of the strategy of Mr. Scott, who made job creation his mantra and is drawing a clear contrast between Florida’s depressed economy in 2010 and its rebounding one today. At every chance, Mr. Crist is repeatedly portrayed as an opportunist who ditched his party and the governorship when he ran for the United States Senate as Florida was deep in recession.
Continue reading the main story
Continue reading the main story
“The economy is doing much better,” Mr. Stipanovich said. “And the governor is getting plenty of traction in saying Charlie led us into the wilderness and he led us out.”
At the campaign rally Ms. Suarez attended, Mr. Scott accused Mr. Crist of “using the Obama playbook” and rattled off then-and-now state unemployment figures, tax obligations and deficits, all of them much improved, he said. He also chuckled about his awkward style on the stump, contrasting himself with the “smooth talker,” Mr. Crist.
“He didn’t want to do the job of running the state of Florida and making this the best place to raise a family,” he said of Mr. Crist.
On the flip side, Mr. Crist said Mr. Scott had favored the wealthy and powerful to the detriment of the poor and the middle class. And he casts Mr. Scott as too conservative for Florida, saying the governor has pushed to curb abortion and voter rights, has failed to acknowledge the threat of global warming and, in his first year in office, drastically cut school funding.
“I understand if you don’t want to talk about Florida, because his record on Florida is terrible,” Mr. Crist recently said of Mr. Scott.
To offset Mr. Scott’s fund-raising advantage, Mr. Crist is focusing on the grass roots, using Mr. Obama’s turnout strategies. Mr. Crist is now rolling out his money on television ads, which should blunt some of Mr. Scott’s attacks. He has also opened 25 field offices.
“Given the amount they have spent, we feel we are in a great position,” said
Omar Khan
, Mr. Crist’s campaign manager.
Rather than duck from his party switch, Mr. Crist and his supporters remind voters that he is a centrist who worked well with Democrats as governor and pushed for changes that sometimes scored him no political points, like making it easier for nonviolent felons to regain the right to vote.
“He did it because he knew it was right and he knew that we are always a country of second chances,” Mr. Clinton told a crowd that was largely African-American, a constituency that has lobbied the state about that issue, in a hotel ballroom here.
By now, the vast majority of Floridians know whom they will choose, analysts said. The fight will play out along the margins in certain swing counties, a pocket of Hispanics here, a group of Tea Party activists there.
The key to success in November for either candidate is turnout — something that analysts said would be easier for Republicans in this midterm election — and luring away independent voters, who make up 25 percent of the electorate. Mr. Crist also needs a large number of African-American and Hispanic votes.
“This whole shebang is going to depend on who shows up,” Mr. Clinton scolded the Democrats in the room. “In the end, it’s on you whether he becomes governor.”

Mentioning the name of Rob Portman, the Ohio senator, as a potential Republican nominee in 2016 gets this reaction, especially from Republicans: “Really?”
Yet there he was last month in New Hampshire
, fueling speculation that he will make a bid for the White House. While there are a lot of obvious reasons to think a moderate Republican who supports same-sex marriage could never win the party nomination, there’s a good deal of data that suggests the opposite. Research on emotion and persuasion suggests that Mr. Portman may be exactly what the party needs to win in 2016 — and beyond.
Mr. Portman has a few potential advantages. The first is that very few people know anything about him. In August 2012, when he was being discussed as a possible running mate for Mitt Romney, many pollsters asked people whether their opinion of Mr. Portman was favorable or unfavorable. Most people had no opinion of him whatsoever. The
CNN/ORC poll
, for example, revealed that 52 percent of the population had “never heard of” Mr. Portman, and another 20 percent had “no opinion” of him. Even among Republicans, 65 percent couldn’t rate him. That’s a big, blank slate.
It may seem counterintuitive, but for Mr. Portman, being unknown is a good thing. It gives him the chance to tell his story from scratch and persuade people to trust him. If it is not obvious why this is a plus, consider being Hillary Rodham Clinton, whom nearly everyone already knows, and who has to convince many people that, despite their predispositions toward her, they should trust her. Only 5 percent of the electorate cannot rate Mrs. Clinton on the same favorability scale.
Being unknown is even better for Mr. Portman than it would be for other candidates, because the story of his
evolution on the topic of gay equality
is personal and emotional. Those qualities of the story are likely to make him seem authentic and sincere, someone voters can trust.
Research in communication studies, psychology and political science has shown that emotion can enhance the impact of political messages in news stories or in ads in compelling ways. Mr. Portman has a tale in his support of gay equality that can evoke an emotional response. The senator’s son told his parents he was gay three years ago, when he was in college. Last year, Mr. Portman announced a change of his position on marriage equality. He, like a majority of Americans, now supports same-sex marriage. Republicans support it less than Democrats or independents, but even so, roughly
4 in 10 Republicans
are supportive.
When he speaks about his transition on the issue, Mr. Portman can be seen as both a father and a husband — not merely a politician. He can come across as a father who wants the same support, love and connection for his son that he has had through his own marriage. It’s a powerful vulnerability and, if done right, may suggest to voters that Mr. Portman will speak honestly to them about other topics as well.
But can he win with a moderate position on same-sex marriage? He will be running in a party whose members thought the 2012 primary battle was a contest to choose “anybody but Romney” — because Mitt Romney was seen as moderate. This belief that moderates are unacceptable, however, turned out to be
more of a myth
than a motto.
In “The Gamble,” John Sides of George Washington University and I used data from the 2012
Cooperative Campaign Analysis Project
to show that Mr. Romney was viewed positively by likely Republican primary voters regardless of whether they were conservatives or moderates, pro-life or pro-choice, relatively wealthy or not, or Tea Party members or not. In fact, Mr. Romney was viewed more favorably among the very constituencies that were supposed to want anyone but him. For example, about 74 percent of conservative Republican primary voters had a favorable view of him, compared with 62 percent of liberals and moderates in the party.
Even if some in the party were not enthusiastic about Mr. Romney’s moderate positions, they were not rejecting him because of it. The same may hold true for Mr. Portman.
